subject: Egress translation & control-plane segregation for Private deploy - overview and next steps
messages:
From: Aisha Rahman <aisha_rahman@redwood.ai>
To: Matthew Hayes <matthew.hayes@nimhealth.com>, laura_bennett@redwood.ai, karthik_iyer@redwood.ai
Date: Tue, 9 Mar 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Egress translation & control-plane segregation for Private deploy - overview and next steps

Hi Matthew —

Thanks again for the discussion this morning. As promised, I attached a concise overview diagram (egress-translation + control-plane segregation) and a short companion PDF calling out the evidence we can provide for SOC 2 / SIG / CAIQ. High-level items covered in the attachments: 
- Egress Translation Layer (ETL): a stateless translation proxy that maps customer VPC egress policies to Redwood egress filters, preserving source IP ranges and applying DPI exceptions where required.
- Control-plane segregation: customer-managed control-plane peering using a mutually authenticated TLS channel, with metadata-only telemetry forwarded over an encrypted, auditable channel.
- Sidecar tenant overlay: per-tenant sidecars for telemetry shims and KV-cache isolation in Private deployments.

Action items I suggest for next week:
1) Karthik to validate the ETL mapping for NimHealth-specific CIDR ranges and confirm required egress ports.
2) Laura to prepare a short SOC 2 evidence list scoped to the control-plane peering (logs, key rotation proof, peering configs).
3) Matthew / NimHealth security to confirm any blocked DPI categories or third-party endpoints that require allowlisting.

Attachments: egress-translation-diagram.png (diagram), control-plane-segmentation.pdf (evidence checklist).

Let me know if you'd prefer a short walkthrough call — we can demo the sidecar behavior and telemetry redaction in 20–30 minutes.

Thanks,

Aisha Rahman

From: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Egress translation & control-plane segregation for Private deploy - overview and next steps

Thanks Aisha — quick notes after looking at the diagram: 

- ETL behavioral modes: allowlist, deny-by-default, and passthrough-with-annotations. For NimHealth we should start with deny-by-default + explicit allowlist for the PACS and SFTP endpoints you mentioned.
- Ports: we need TCP 443, 22 (SFTP only), and 3389 is explicitly blocked per previous notes; I'll add port-level ACL samples to the diagram legend.
- MTU and fragmentation: the sidecar adds ~76 bytes of overhead when performing per-flow metadata stamping; if NimHealth uses jumbo frames we should reflect that in the MTU guidance.

I'll update the diagram and upload a revised PNG today (will reference in the drive link). Laura — once I update, can you drop the list of logs we can export (control-plane handshake logs, ETL decision logs, sidecar audit events) so NimHealth has the SOC 2 evidence mapping?

Karthik
Principal Network Security Engineer | Redwood Inference

Aisha, Karthik — thanks for the quick turnaround. A few follow-ups from our security team after reviewing the attachments: 

1) Can you confirm whether the ETL performs any FQDN rewriting or just policy evaluation? Our procurement requires no hostname rewriting unless explicitly consented.
2) Telemetry: "metadata-only" needs to be spelled out — what fields are considered metadata? We need confirmation that no PHI or patient identifiers are ever included.
3) Key management: for the mutually authenticated TLS channel, do you support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM)? If so, can you provide an example of a key rotation event and the artifacts (audit log entry, new cert fingerprint) we would receive?

We also have a SIG questionnaire in progress — would prefer to map the control-plane peering questions to your CAIQ responses. Can you provide a quick mapping doc or an outline of which CAIQ control IDs this design satisfies?

If helpful, our security engineer, Claire (security@nimhealth.com), is available Thursday afternoon for a 30-minute call.

Thanks,
Matthew Hayes\Director of IT, NimHealth
matthew.hayes@nimhealth.com

From: Aisha Rahman <aisha_rahman@redwood.ai>
To: Matthew Hayes <matthew.hayes@nimhealth.com>, NimHealth Security <security@nimhealth.com>, laura_bennett@redwood.ai, karthik_iyer@redwood.ai
Date: Thu, 11 Mar 2027 14:47:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Egress translation & control-plane segregation for Private deploy - overview and next steps

Matthew / Claire — appreciate the detailed questions. Short answers below and next steps: 

1) FQDN handling: ETL does NOT rewrite hostnames by default. It evaluates policies against FQDNs and IPs; rewriting is an opt-in transformation mode (we only enable it with customer-confirmed consent and document it in the CAIQ addendum).

2) Metadata fields (examples): timestamp, source tenant id (opaque GUID), flow-class label (e.g., inference-output, model-checkpoint), byte counts, and ETL decision code. We explicitly strip request bodies and any headers flagged as PHI. We will provide a short schema doc and a sample sanitized telemetry record for Claire to review.

3) KMS/HSM support: yes — Private deployments support customer-managed keys via KMIP-compatible HSMs or cloud KMS (AES-256 keys with RSA/ECDSA certs for TLS). We will include a sample rotation artifact (audit log entry + cert fingerprint) in the SOC 2 packet.

Mapping to CAIQ/SIG: Laura will draft a mapping table that ties the control-plane peering and ETL behaviors to specific CAIQ control IDs (networking and key mgmt sections), plus a short SIG answer template for common Qs.

Next steps (proposed):
- Thu 11 Mar 16:00 PT — 30m sync with Claire to walk through the diagram and telemetry sample (we can do remote screenshare + live demo of the sidecar redaction).
- By Fri 12 Mar EOD — Karthik uploads updated diagram with port-level ACLs and MTU notes; Laura uploads CAIQ mapping stub and the SOC 2 evidence list.

I will add the NimHealth contact to the Drive folder and share a DocuSign link only if we get to the peering agreement stage (we typically record peering under our standard Private Deployment Addendum).

Thanks,
